## Objectives

+ Read a chart and say what it does — and does not — support.
+ Tell *discrete* data from *continuous* data, and say why it changes the
  chart — and, later, the probability distribution.
+ Construct and interpret a *frequency distribution* and *histogram*,
  grouped and ungrouped.
+ Construct and interpret *ogives* and *cumulative* frequencies.
+ Display qualitative data using *bar charts* and *pie charts*.
+ Display quality issues with a *Pareto chart*.
+ Organize two variables in a *contingency table* and read a *heatmap*.
+ Present a distribution with a *stem and leaf* display.
+ Show the relationship between two variables using a *scatter plot*, and
  say which variable belongs on which axis.
+ Recognize the ways a technically correct chart can still mislead.
+ Notice when two variables are not in comparable *units*, and say what the
  comparison is actually measuring.
+ Specify a chart or a frequency distribution precisely enough that an AI
  assistant can build it in Excel — and verify what comes back.

The code that draws each chart is folded away. Click **Show the code** if you
are curious, but nothing in this chapter is assessed on your ability to write
it. What is assessed is whether you can look at the output and say what it
means.

## The role technology plays in statistics

Hardcore statisticians are perfectly happy to receive large quantities of data
in tabular formats. Likely this is because they know how to import the data
into their preferred statistical interface and can perform their own analysis
on it. Artificial intelligence tools are cutting the gap between what requires
a hardcore statistician and what an interested person can do.

Senior leaders often have the analytical ability to draw insight from raw
data. What they do not have is the time. Even traditional descriptive
statistics — **mean**, **median**, **quartiles**, **minimum** and **maximum** —
take more effort to interpret than many will spend. That is a particular
challenge when your goal is to *persuade*. We do not want our audience's eyes
to glaze over. We want to make the case from the data as elegantly as
possible.

This brings us to **data visualization**: presenting data so that its
important features are clear. This takes skill. There are many chart types to
choose from, and some are far better than others at showing a particular
pattern. AI is a genuine boon to producing them — and no help at all in
deciding which one is honest.

## Seeing a pattern that a table hides

### Two centuries of data, as a table

Here is the Maddison Project's estimate of GDP per capita, for every country
it covers, for every year it covers.

```{python}
#| label: gdp-panel-size
print(f"{len(gdp_panel):,} rows")
print(f"{gdp_panel['entity'].nunique()} countries and regions")
print(f"years {gdp_panel['year'].min()} to {gdp_panel['year'].max()}")
print()
print(gdp_panel.head(10).to_string(index=False))
```

Ten of twenty-one thousand rows. Nobody is going to read this, and printing
more of it would not help. So narrow it all the way down — one row per
observation for the *world*, with the share of people living in extreme
poverty beside it.

```{python}
#| label: world-table
show = pd.DataFrame({
    "Year": world.year,
    "GDP per capita": world.gdp_pc,
    "% in extreme poverty": world.share_poor,
    "In poverty (millions)": (world.n_poor / 1e6),
    "World population (millions)": ((world.n_poor + world.n_notpoor) / 1e6),
})
print(show.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.1f}"))
```

**Ten rows.** This one you can read, and reading it tells you two things
immediately: income went up, and the share in poverty went down.

Now say what *shape* that relationship has. Is it steady? Does it accelerate?
Does it flatten out at high incomes? Is it tight, or is it loose with a lot of
exceptions?

You cannot answer any of that from the table, and the table is only ten rows
long. This is the part worth being precise about: **the table is not hiding
the facts. It is hiding the structure.**

### The same ten rows, drawn

```{python}
#| label: poverty-connected
_ = connected_scatter(world["gdp_pc"], world["share_poor"],
                      labels=world["year"], logx=True,
                      title="Extreme poverty and income, the world 1820 to 2015",
                      xlab="GDP per capita (international-$, 2011 prices, log scale)",
                      ylab="Share living in extreme poverty (%)")
```

Neither axis is time. Both variables are measured quantities, and the points
are joined in the order they happened — so the line is the path the world has
travelled through two centuries. It goes one way.

```{python}
#| label: poverty-headline
first, last = world.iloc[0], world.iloc[-1]
for row in (first, last):
    pop = row.n_poor + row.n_notpoor
    print(f"{int(row.year)}   {row.share_poor:5.1f}% in extreme poverty   "
          f"GDP per capita ${row.gdp_pc:,.0f}   "
          f"world population {pop/1e9:.2f} billion")
```

::: {.scarlet}
In 1820, **nine people in ten** on this planet lived in extreme poverty. By
2015, **one in ten** did.

There is no precedent for that in recorded history, and no table of ten rows
makes you feel it.
:::

### How strong is it, and why the axis is logarithmic

```{python}
#| label: poverty-correlation
print(f"correlation of poverty share with GDP per capita       "
      f"r = {world['share_poor'].corr(world['gdp_pc']):+.3f}")
print(f"correlation of poverty share with LOG GDP per capita   "
      f"r = {world['share_poor'].corr(np.log(world['gdp_pc'])):+.3f}")
```

Both are strong. The second is stronger, and that is the justification for the
log axis rather than a decorative preference: income spans more than an order
of magnitude over this period — from about \$1,100 to about \$15,000 — and the
relationship is closer to straight when income is expressed in *multiples*
rather than in dollars.

::: {.charcoal}
This is a real choice, and it belongs in the "charts that mislead" discussion
later in this chapter as much as here. On a linear axis the same ten points
bunch up at the left and the last century dominates the picture. On a log axis
they spread evenly and the whole two hundred years is legible.

Neither version is false. They answer different questions, and the axis is
where you decide which question you are asking.
:::

### The number that did not fall

Now the harder half of the same data, from the same two columns.

```{python}
#| label: poverty-counts
peak = world.loc[world["n_poor"].idxmax()]
print(f"Number of people in extreme poverty")
print(f"  1820   {first.n_poor/1e6:>7,.0f} million")
print(f"  {int(peak.year)}   {peak.n_poor/1e6:>7,.0f} million   <- the peak")
print(f"  2015   {last.n_poor/1e6:>7,.0f} million")
print()
print(f"The SHARE fell from {first.share_poor:.1f}% to {last.share_poor:.1f}%.")
print(f"The COUNT fell by only "
      f"{100*(1 - last.n_poor/first.n_poor):.0f}%.")
print(f"World population grew "
      f"{(last.n_poor+last.n_notpoor)/(first.n_poor+first.n_notpoor):.1f} times.")
```

The number of people living in extreme poverty **peaked in 1980**, at nearly
two billion — more than twice the 1820 figure — during a period when the
*share* was falling the whole time. And in 2015 it was still 733 million
people.

::: {.scarlet}
Both of these are true, computed from the same two columns:

> Extreme poverty has almost been eliminated — it fell from 89% to 10%.

> Seven hundred and thirty-three million people still live in extreme poverty,
> barely fewer than in 1820.

Which one you put in the caption decides what your reader believes, and
neither one is a lie. This is the Valentine's Day pie chart from later in this
chapter, at world-historical scale: **the arithmetic is not the argument. The
choice of denominator is.**
:::

### What this chart is, and what it is not

Four things belong in the provenance record before anyone quotes a number off
it.

```{python}
#| label: poverty-provenance
print("Poverty : World population living in extreme poverty")
print("          Ravallion (2016), updated with World Bank (2019), via")
print("          Our World in Data")
print("Line    : $1.90 per day, international-$ at 2011 prices")
print("Income  : Maddison Project Database 2023 (Bolt and van Zanden),")
print("          constant international-$ at 2011 prices, via Our World in Data")
print(f"Coverage: {int(world.year.min())} to {int(world.year.max())}, "
      f"{len(world)} observations")
```

1. **The poverty line here is superseded.** These figures use \$1.90 a day at
   2011 prices. The World Bank has since moved to \$2.15 at 2017 prices and
   then to \$3.00 at 2021 prices. Each revision changes how many people are
   counted as extremely poor without anyone's circumstances changing at all —
   the same lesson as the two consumer confidence series later in this
   chapter, applied to the most-quoted statistic in development economics.

2. **The early numbers are reconstructions, not measurements.** Nobody
   surveyed household consumption in 1820. The figure is modelled from
   national accounts and distribution estimates, and different teams have
   published different reconstructions — some put 1820 nearer three-quarters
   than nine-tenths. **The level is uncertain. The direction is not.**

3. **It stops in 2015**, because that is where this particular series stops.

4. **It is a time path, not a comparison of countries.** The claim it supports
   is about the world getting richer and less poor together over two hundred
   years. It is *not* the claim that a rich country today has less poverty than
   a poor one — that would need a different chart, drawn from the country panel
   rather than the world row.

::: {.charcoal}
With all four caveats stated, the finding survives every one of them. That is
what a robust result looks like: you can attack the poverty line, the
reconstruction method, the end date and the units, and the picture does not
change shape.

Hold on to that, because the next chart in this chapter does not survive its
first caveat at all.
:::

## And here is a chart that looks like a pattern

### The data for this one

A different data set: a panel of the 50 US states carrying a house price
index, its change over the past decade, the unemployment rate, current
population, and population growth over the past decade.

```{python}
#| label: state-head
states.head(8)
```

```{python}
#| label: state-summary
states[["HPI", "gHPI", "UR", "POPN", "gPOP"]].describe().round(2)
```

Before reading anything into those numbers, one check carried over from
Chapter 1:

```{python}
#| label: as-of-dates
for col, label in [("HPI_date", "House price index"),
                   ("UR_date", "Unemployment rate"),
                   ("POP_date", "Population")]:
    dates = pd.to_datetime(states[col])
    print(f"{label:<22} as of {dates.max().date()}  "
          f"({'all states agree' if dates.nunique() == 1 else 'DATES DIFFER'})")

print()
print("Both growth rates cover ten years -- but not the same ten years:")
hpi_end = pd.to_datetime(states["HPI_date"]).max()
hpi_start = pd.to_datetime(states["HPIO_date"]).max()
pop_end = pd.to_datetime(states["POP_date"]).max()
pop_start = pop_end - pd.DateOffset(years=10)
print(f"  House price growth   {hpi_start.date()} to {hpi_end.date()}")
print(f"  Population growth    {pop_start.date()} to {pop_end.date()}")
```

::: {.scarlet}
These variables are measured **as of different dates**, spanning more than a
year, and the two ten-year windows are offset from each other by about a year.
Every chart in this chapter puts them side by side anyway. That is normal
practice, and it is a limitation you should state rather than hide — house
prices from one quarter and unemployment from six months later are not a
snapshot of a single moment.
:::

Here is average house price index by unemployment rate, in equal-width bins.

```{python}
#| label: hpi-by-ur
_ = binned_bar(states["UR"], states["HPI"], bins=6,
               title="Average house price index by unemployment rate",
               xlab="Unemployment rate bin (%)", ylab="House price index")
```

There is no pattern here worth reporting. The bars wander. Note the `n=`
labels: some bins hold a handful of states, and a bar computed from four
observations should not be read as though it were computed from twenty.

Now the same chart against population growth.

```{python}
#| label: hpi-by-gpop
_ = binned_bar(states["gPOP"], states["HPI"], bins=6,
               title="Average house price index by population growth",
               xlab="Population growth over the decade (%)",
               ylab="House price index")
```

This one does look like something: states with faster population growth tend
to have higher house price indexes. Before believing it, ask how strong "tend
to" is.

```{python}
#| label: correlations
for col, label in [("UR", "unemployment rate"),
                   ("POPN", "population"),
                   ("gPOP", "population growth")]:
    print(f"Correlation of house price INDEX with {label:<20} "
          f"r = {states['HPI'].corr(states[col]):+.3f}")
```

A correlation of +0.30 is a real relationship and a weak one. That is a fine
place to stop — most analyses do. Let us not stop there, because there is
something wrong with the question.

### Look at which states are at the top

```{python}
#| label: hpi-extremes
top = states.nlargest(6, "HPI")[["Member", "HPI", "gPOP"]]
bottom = states.nsmallest(6, "HPI")[["Member", "HPI", "gPOP"]]
print("Highest house price index")
print(top.to_string(index=False))
print("\nLowest house price index")
print(bottom.to_string(index=False))
print("\nFastest-growing states, and where they rank on the index")
fast = states.nlargest(6, "gPOP")[["Member", "gPOP", "HPI"]]
print(fast.to_string(index=False))
```

Massachusetts, New York and Rhode Island lead a chart supposedly about
housing, and they are among the slowest-growing states in the country.
Texas grew 15.4% and sits in the bottom half. Idaho grew 22.8% — the fastest
in the nation — and is nowhere near the top.

Something is wrong. Read the series documentation.

```{python}
#| label: hpi-provenance
print("Series     : {ST}STHPI, one per state")
print("Name       : All-Transactions House Price Index")
print("Source     : U.S. Federal Housing Finance Agency, via FRED")
print("Units      : Index, 1980 Q1 = 100")
print("Frequency  : Quarterly")
```

::: {.scarlet}
**Index, 1980 Q1 = 100.** Every state starts at 100 in 1980 by construction.
So a state's index *level* does not measure what a house costs there. It
measures **how much prices have risen since 1980** — cumulative appreciation
over forty-five years.

Massachusetts is at the top because Massachusetts has appreciated the most
since 1980, not because it is expensive today. The chart is not a housing
price chart at all. It is a chart of forty-five-year growth, being compared
against ten-year growth.
:::

This is the same failure as the consumer confidence series later in this
chapter: two correct numbers, describing the same reality, that are not
comparable because they were constructed differently. Here it is worse in one
way — nothing in the file says so. The column is labelled `HPI` and every
value in it is right.

### The fix is to compare like with like

`gPOP` is a **ten-year change**. So compare it to the **ten-year change in the
index**, which is a percentage and is comparable across states.

```{python}
#| label: hpi-change-by-gpop
_ = binned_bar(states["gPOP"], states["gHPI"], bins=6,
               title="Average ten-year house price growth by population growth",
               xlab="Population growth over the decade (%)",
               ylab="House price growth over the decade (%)")
```

```{python}
#| label: correlations-fixed
pairs = [("HPI", "gPOP", "house price INDEX LEVEL", "population growth"),
         ("gHPI", "gPOP", "house price CHANGE (10y)", "population growth"),
         ("gHPI", "UR", "house price CHANGE (10y)", "unemployment rate")]
for ycol, xcol, ylab, xlab in pairs:
    print(f"{ylab:<26} vs {xlab:<20} r = {states[ycol].corr(states[xcol]):+.3f}")
```

::: {.charcoal}
Same fifty states. Same source. Same download. The correlation went from
**+0.30 to +0.71** because the units changed, and nothing else did.

The unemployment rate is still flat against the new variable — r of about
zero. That matters: it says the improvement is not an artefact of making
everything correlate with everything. One pairing got much stronger and the
other did not move.
:::

### And now be careful again

A correlation of +0.71 is strong enough that people will start saying causal
things about it. It still does not license them.

```{python}
#| label: scatter-fixed
_ = scatter(states["gPOP"], states["gHPI"],
            labels=states["Member"],
            title="Ten-year house price growth and population growth, US states",
            xlab="Population growth over the decade (%)",
            ylab="House price growth over the decade (%)")
```

The scatter shows what the bar chart cannot: real spread, and obvious
exceptions. Maine and New Hampshire grew slowly and appreciated enormously.
North Dakota grew faster than average and appreciated less than almost anyone.
Compare this with the binned bar chart above, where those states disappeared
into an average.

::: {.charcoal}
**Binning averages away the disagreement.** Both charts are honest; the
scatter is more informative about how much confidence the pattern deserves.

And the strongest claim either one supports is still: *states with faster
population growth tended to see faster house price growth over the same
decade.* Not that population growth raised prices. People may be moving toward
places where prices are rising, prices may be rising where people are moving,
or a third factor — climate, taxes, industry, land-use rules — may drive both.
**The chart cannot tell you which, and neither can r = 0.71.**
:::

### The window is a choice too

One more thing to be suspicious of. Ten years was not handed to us; we picked
it. Here is the same comparison over five years.

```{python}
#| label: window-choice
print("Correlation of population growth with house price growth")
for col, window in [("gHPI", "ten years"), ("gHPI5", "five years")]:
    print(f"  measured over {window:<11} r = {states['gPOP'].corr(states[col]):+.3f}")

print()
print("Spread of house price growth across the fifty states:")
for col, window in [("gHPI", "ten years"), ("gHPI5", "five years")]:
    print(f"  over {window:<11} {states[col].min():6.1f}% to {states[col].max():6.1f}%   "
          f"(standard deviation {states[col].std():.1f})")
```

Over five years the relationship all but disappears — and the second table
says why. After 2021 essentially every state's prices rose, and they rose by
similar amounts, so there is very little variation left across states for
anything to explain.

::: {.scarlet}
A relationship that is strong over one window and absent over another has not
been discovered. It has been *found in a particular window*, and the window
belongs in the sentence: "over the decade to 2026." Anyone who reports the
number without the window is reporting something they cannot support.
:::

## Displaying quantitative data

### Two kinds of number

Before any of this, a distinction that decides how the rest of the chapter
behaves — and which will still be deciding things in Chapter 5 and Chapter 6.

**Discrete data** are values that have been *counted*. They are restricted to
whole numbers. The number of quarters in which house prices fell, the number
of employees who left last month, the number of defective units in a batch:
you cannot have 3.4 of any of them.

**Continuous data** are values that have been *measured*. They can take any
real number within their range, limited only by the precision of the
instrument. Population growth of 6.3%, a hold time of 4.82 minutes, a
temperature of 76.4 degrees.

::: {.charcoal}
**The acid test.** Ask: *how many values are possible inside a given interval?*

Between 0 and 3, a count can take four values — 0, 1, 2, 3. A measurement can
take infinitely many: 2.0, 2.04, 2.046, and on forever.

A finite answer means discrete. An infinite answer means continuous.
:::

Counted or measured is the question, and it is not always the same as "does
the number happen to be a whole number today."

```{python}
#| label: discrete-or-continuous
for label, kind, why in [
        ("Quarters in which a state's house prices fell", "discrete",
         "counted; there is no 3.4th quarter"),
        ("Population growth over the decade (%)", "continuous",
         "measured; 6.31 and 6.312 are both possible"),
        ("Days the US spent in recession", "discrete", "counted"),
        ("Consumer confidence index", "continuous", "measured on a scale"),
        ("Respondents choosing each poll answer", "discrete", "counted"),
        ("Unemployment rate (%)", "continuous", "a measured proportion")]:
    print(f"{label:<46} {kind:<11} {why}")
```

::: {.scarlet}
**The awkward middle.** Some variables are technically discrete and are
displayed as though they were continuous, and this is normal practice rather
than a mistake.

A golf score is counted in strokes, so it is discrete. Annual income is
counted in cents. Age is counted in years. But when the range is wide and the
steps are tiny relative to it — scores from 279 to 308, incomes from \$40,000
to \$88,000 — grouping them into classes and drawing them as continuous is
both conventional and more readable.

The test that matters in practice is not "is this technically discrete" but
**"are there few enough distinct values that each one can be its own class?"**
Six values, yes. Three hundred, no.
:::

### A frequency distribution with one class per value

When the distinct values are few, each value gets its own class and nothing is
grouped at all. Here is a genuine count, from the same fifty states.

For each state, we took the last ten years of the quarterly house price index —
forty quarterly changes — and counted how many of them were **negative**. How
many times in a decade did that state's housing market go backwards?

```{python}
#| label: freq-discrete
frequency_table(states["nDOWN"], bins="each", cumulative=True)
```

No bins were chosen, no width was decided, no boundary had to be argued over.
The values *are* the classes. This is the simplest frequency distribution
there is, and it is the one the textbook builds first.

Read it straight off. **Thirty of the fifty states — 60% — had three or fewer
falling quarters in a decade.**

```{python}
#| label: down-extremes
v = states["nDOWN"]
print(f"n = {len(v)} states, {int(v.min())} to {int(v.max())} falling quarters")
print(f"mean {v.mean():.2f}   median {v.median():.0f}\n")
print("Never fell:  " + ", ".join(states.loc[v == v.min(), "Member"]))
print("Fell most:   " + ", ".join(states.loc[v == v.max(), "Member"])
      + f" ({int(v.max())} of 40 quarters)")
print("\nStates with exactly 6 falling quarters: "
      + (", ".join(states.loc[v == 6, "Member"]) or "none"))
```

### The class that isn't there

Look again at the row for **6**. Its frequency is zero.

That row is easy to delete and tempting to delete, and deleting it would be
wrong. A class with no observations in it is a *finding* — it says something
about the shape of the distribution. Leave it in, and the reader can see that
the distribution has a gap in it. Take it out, and the 5 and the 7 sit next to
each other as though nothing were missing.

::: {.charcoal}
This is the same instinct as Tukey's rule for stem and leaf displays, later in
this chapter: **don't cut your leafless stems.** An empty class and an empty
stem are the same thing, and both should stay.

It is also the fourth rule of building grouped classes — *avoid empty classes*
— seen from the other side. That rule is about not choosing a class width so
narrow that you manufacture empty classes. This one is about not hiding an
empty class you did not manufacture.
:::

### Drawing it: the gap between the bars

```{python}
#| label: discrete-hist
_ = discrete_histogram(states["nDOWN"],
                       title="Quarters with falling house prices, last ten years",
                       xlab="Number of falling quarters (out of 40)")
```

Notice the **gaps between the bars**. That is not a styling choice. It is a
convention with a meaning:

| Data | Bars | Because |
|------|------|---------|
| **Discrete** | separated | nothing exists between 2 and 3, so nothing is drawn there |
| **Continuous** | touching | every value between 2 and 3 exists and belongs to some class |

Here are both, side by side, from this same data set.

```{python}
#| label: gaps-convention
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.2))

vals = sorted(states["nDOWN"].unique())
allv = list(range(int(min(vals)), int(max(vals)) + 1))
axes[0].bar(allv, [int((states["nDOWN"] == v).sum()) for v in allv],
            width=0.55, color=UNLV_SCARLET, alpha=0.85)
axes[0].set_xticks(allv)
axes[0].set_title("DISCRETE: falling quarters (a count)\nbars separated",
                  fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Number of falling quarters")

axes[1].hist(states["gPOP"], bins=np.arange(-5, 30, 5), color=UNLV_SCARLET,
             alpha=0.85, edgecolor="white")
axes[1].set_title("CONTINUOUS: population growth (a measurement)\nbars touching",
                  fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Population growth over the decade (%)")

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6")
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A reader who knows the convention learns what kind of variable they are
looking at before reading a single label. A reader who does not still gets the
counts right. **You lose nothing by following it and you mislead people by
breaking it** — Excel, left alone, will draw a continuous variable with gaps
and a discrete one without, and it is on you to fix it.

::: {.scarlet}
**Why this outlives Chapter 2.** Counted-or-measured is not a charting detail.
It is the fork the rest of the course runs on.

**Chapter 5** builds probability distributions for *discrete* variables, where
you can ask "what is the probability of exactly 3?" and get a real answer.
**Chapter 6** builds them for *continuous* variables, where the probability of
exactly any single value is zero and every question has to be asked about an
*interval* instead.

The same question — "what is the chance of getting 3?" — is sensible in one
chapter and meaningless in the other. Which chapter you are in is decided by
the distinction on this page.
:::

### When the values have to be grouped

Fifty states produced counts spanning ten whole numbers, nine of which
actually occurred — few enough that one class per value worked. Now take a
*measured* variable from the same file.

```{python}
#| label: distinct-values
for col, label in [("nDOWN", "Falling quarters (counted)"),
                   ("gPOP", "Population growth % (measured)")]:
    print(f"{label:<34} {states[col].nunique():>2} distinct values "
          f"among {len(states)} states")
```

Population growth has almost as many distinct values as it has states. One
class per value would give a table of forty-odd rows, most of them holding a
single state, which is a list of the raw data with extra steps.

So the values get **grouped**: several of them share a class.

A **frequency distribution** counts how many values fall in each range, or
*bin*. Here is population growth across the 50 states.

```{python}
#| label: freq-table
frequency_table(states["gPOP"], bins=np.arange(-5, 30, 5), cumulative=True)
```

The **PCT** column is the *relative frequency*: the count in each class divided
by the total. There are 50 states, so a class holding 17 of them is
$17/50 = 34\%$.

The **CUM_PCT** column is the *cumulative relative frequency*, totalling as
you move down. Its interpretation is direct: **44% of states grew by 5% or
less over the decade, and 72% grew by 10% or less.** Only one state exceeded
20%.

A **histogram** draws the same information.

```{python}
#| label: histogram
_ = histogram(states["gPOP"], bins=np.arange(-5, 30, 5),
              title="Distribution of state population growth",
              xlab="Population growth over the decade (%)")
```

```{python}
#| label: skew-check
g = states["gPOP"]
print(f"mean   {g.mean():6.2f}")
print(f"median {g.median():6.2f}")
print(f"The mean sits {'above' if g.mean() > g.median() else 'below'} the median, "
      f"by {abs(g.mean() - g.median()):.2f} points.")
print(f"\nFastest growing: {states.loc[g.idxmax(), 'Member']} at {g.max():.1f}%")
print(f"Slowest growing: {states.loc[g.idxmin(), 'Member']} at {g.min():.1f}%")
```

This is an **asymmetrical** distribution. A *symmetrical* one would be a mirror
image on either side of the middle. Here most of the mass sits at the left and
a thin tail stretches right — a few fast-growing states pull the mean above the
median. That gap between mean and median *is* the skew, expressed as a number.

::: {.charcoal}
When a distribution is skewed, the mean and the median answer different
questions. The median describes the typical state. The mean is pulled by the
extremes. Reporting only one, without saying which, is how a summary becomes
misleading without containing a false number.
:::

### The ogive

The **ogive** plots the cumulative relative frequency. A point on the line
reads: this percent of observations fall at or below that value.

```{python}
#| label: ogive
_ = ogive(states["gPOP"], bins=np.arange(-5, 30, 5),
          title="Cumulative distribution of state population growth",
          xlab="Population growth over the decade (%)")
```

The dotted line marks 50%. Where the curve crosses it is the median. A steep
section means many observations packed into a narrow range; a flat section
means few.

## How many classes?

For grouped data we have to choose the number of classes. A common
rule-of-thumb is to find $k$ such that

$$2^k \geq n,$$

where $n$ is the number of observations and $k$ the number of classes. With 50
states, $2^5 = 32$ and $2^6 = 64$, so $k = 6$.

The class width then follows from the range divided by the number of classes.
This is a *rule of thumb*, not a law — and the choice has consequences, as the
next section shows.

### Rules when constructing grouped classes

1. **Equal-size classes.** Unequal widths make patterns misleading.
2. **Mutually exclusive classes.** Boundaries must not overlap.
3. **Include all data values.** Fifty observations, fifty observations placed.
4. **Avoid empty classes.** Too-narrow widths produce classes with no data.
5. **Avoid open-ended classes** where possible — though sometimes an age class
   of "19+" beats fifty empty classes between 19 and 70.

## Displaying qualitative data

From December 1854 the NBER recession indicator marks every day as recession or
not. That is *qualitative* data: each day carries a label.

```{python}
#| label: recession-overall
print(f"{len(recessions):,} days, {recessions.date.min().date()} "
      f"to {recessions.date.max().date()}")
print(f"Days in recession: {recessions.recession.sum():,} "
      f"({100 * recessions.recession.mean():.1f}%)")
```

```{python}
#| label: recession-bar
counts = recessions.recession.value_counts().sort_index()
_ = bar_chart(["Not recession", "Recession"], counts.to_numpy(),
              title="US economic state, 1854 to today",
              xlab="Economic state", ylab="Days")
```

A single bar chart of the whole period hides the more interesting fact.

```{python}
#| label: recession-eras
d = recessions.set_index("date")
early = d.loc[:"1939-12-31", "recession"].mean()
modern = d.loc["1980-01-01":, "recession"].mean()
print(f"1854 - 1939    {100 * early:5.1f}% of days in recession")
print(f"1980 - present {100 * modern:5.1f}% of days in recession")
print(f"\nRatio: {early / modern:.1f} times more likely before 1940.")
```

```{python}
#| label: recession-decade
by_decade = (recessions.assign(decade=(recessions.date.dt.year // 10 * 10))
             .query("1860 <= decade < 2020")
             .groupby("decade")["recession"].mean() * 100)
_ = bar_chart([f"{int(d)}s" for d in by_decade.index], by_decade.to_numpy(),
              title="Percent of days in recession, by decade",
              xlab="Decade", ylab="Percent of days")
```

The 1870s stand out at 64% — the Long Depression. The 2010s recorded zero
recession days. Reading a chart well means noticing both the shape and the
outliers, then asking what produced them.

## Pareto charts

A **Pareto chart** is a bar chart sorted from most to least frequent, with a
cumulative percentage line. Named for
[Vilfredo Pareto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilfredo_Pareto), it answers
"how few categories account for how much?"

We use the *Monmouth University National Poll #240*, January 2021. Question 16
asked which statement came closest to the respondent's view:

> 1. Our system of government is basically sound and essentially needs no changes
> 2. Our system is basically sound, but needs some improvement
> 3. Our system is not too sound and needs many improvements
> 4. Our system is not sound at all and needs significant changes

```{python}
#| label: pareto
_ = pareto_chart(poll["q16_system_of_government"],
                 title="Views on the American system of government",
                 xlab="Response", ylab="Respondents")
```

Read the black line, not just the bars. The two most common answers account for
over three-quarters of respondents. A summary that reported only the modal
response would miss that the second category is nearly as large.

## Pie charts, and a trap

Pie charts have been the subject of a
[smear campaign](https://www.businessinsider.com/pie-charts-are-the-worst-2013-6).
The criticism has merit: beyond three or four slices, people cannot compare
angles reliably.

Question 38 asked: *Looking ahead to Valentine's Day next month, will you and
your partner do anything special to mark the day?*

```{python}
#| label: q38-freq
q38 = frequency_table(poll["q38_valentines_plans"], cumulative=True)
q38
```

```{python}
#| label: q38-pie
answered = poll["q38_valentines_plans"].dropna()
counts = answered.value_counts().sort_index()
_ = pie_chart(counts.index, counts.to_numpy(),
              title="Valentine's Day plans")
```

::: {.scarlet}
**Look at what that chart is not telling you.** Question 16 was answered by
all 809 respondents. Question 38 was answered by 551. The other 258 were never
asked — the question presupposes a partner.
:::

```{python}
#| label: q38-missing
for q, label in [("q16_system_of_government", "Q16 (system of government)"),
                 ("q38_valentines_plans", "Q38 (Valentine's plans)")]:
    s = poll[q]
    print(f"{label:<32} answered {s.notna().sum():>4}   "
          f"not answered {s.isna().sum():>4}")
```

Every number in that pie chart is correct. Every percentage is correctly
computed. And a reader who sees it captioned "Valentine's Day Plans" will
conclude something about *Americans*, when it describes only the 68% who were
asked. **The chart does not lie. The caption does.**

The honest version says what the base is: *"Among the 551 respondents with a
partner…"*

## Contingency tables

A **contingency table** shows frequencies for two variables at once.

```{python}
#| label: contingency
table = contingency_table(states["gPOP"], states["gHPI"],
                          x_bins=5, y_bins=5,
                          x_name="Population growth (%)",
                          y_name="House price growth (%)")
table
```

```{python}
#| label: heatmap
_ = heatmap(table, title="House price growth and population growth, 50 states",
            xlab="Population growth over the decade (%)",
            ylab="House price growth over the decade (%)")
```

Colour intensity shows where states concentrate. With 50 observations spread
over 25 cells, most cells hold zero, one, or two states — which is itself the
finding. **A heatmap of a small sample looks authoritative and carries very
little information.** Check the counts before reading a pattern into the
colours.

## Stem and leaf display

[John Tukey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Tukey) originated the **stem
and leaf display** in the 1970s, when it could be built by hand. Its virtue is
that every individual observation stays visible, unlike a histogram.

One rule carries over from the empty class earlier in this chapter: **do not
cut your leafless stems.** If no observation falls on a stem, the stem still
appears, empty. Removing it closes a gap that is really there and misstates
the shape of the distribution.

```{python}
#| label: cci-two-files
for name, frame in [("consumer_confidence.csv", cci),
                    ("consumer_confidence_discontinued.csv", cci_old)]:
    print(f"{name}")
    print(f"   rows              {len(frame):,}")
    print(f"   first observation {frame.date.min().date()}")
    print(f"   last observation  {frame.date.max().date()}")
    print(f"   any missing       {int(frame.cci.isna().sum())}")
    print()
```

Two files. Same concept — US consumer confidence, monthly, from 1960. Both
downloaded without error. Both parsed cleanly. Neither has a missing value.
Every number in both is correct.

One of them stopped being published.

```{python}
#| label: cci-staleness
today = pd.Timestamp.today()
for name, frame in [("consumer_confidence.csv", cci),
                    ("consumer_confidence_discontinued.csv", cci_old)]:
    months = (today - frame.date.max()).days / 30.4
    verdict = "CURRENT" if months < 7 else f"STALE by {months:.0f} months"
    print(f"{name:<42} {verdict}")
```

::: {.scarlet}
Nothing in the file contents distinguishes a live series from a dead one. Row
counts look similar, values look plausible, no errors are raised.
**The last observation date is the only tell**, and checking it is the
verification almost nobody performs.

A retired series produces a perfectly reasonable-looking analysis of a world
that no longer exists.
:::

### The same thing, measured on two different scales

The two series do not merely resemble each other. Over the months they both
cover, they move together almost perfectly.

```{python}
#| label: cci-overlap
overlap = cci.merge(cci_old, on="date", suffixes=("_new", "_old")).dropna()

print(f"Overlapping months: {len(overlap):,}")
print(f"Correlation over the overlap: {overlap.cci_new.corr(overlap.cci_old):.3f}")
print()
print(f"{'':<12}{'current':>12}{'retired':>12}")
for label, a, b in [("minimum", cci.cci.min(), cci_old.cci.min()),
                    ("mean", cci.cci.mean(), cci_old.cci.mean()),
                    ("maximum", cci.cci.max(), cci_old.cci.max())]:
    print(f"{label:<12}{a:>12.2f}{b:>12.2f}")
print()
print("The same four months, read from each series:")
print(overlap.tail(4).to_string(index=False))
```

A correlation of 0.992 says these two series carry the same information. The
summary table says they are built differently. The retired series is a
*standardised index*, normalised to a long-run mean of exactly 100, never
straying more than about three points from it. The current series is a
**percentage balance** — roughly, the share of optimistic responses minus the
share of pessimistic ones — and it ranges from the high forties to above 120.

These are not the same measurement rescaled. They are two different ways of
turning the same survey into a number.

::: {.scarlet}
In October 2023 one of these series reads about 69 and the other about 98.
Same month, same concept, same underlying survey.

A student who saw 98 in an old report and 69 in a new one would conclude that
consumer confidence had collapsed. Nothing collapsed. **The normalisation
changed.**
:::

This is why *units* belong in the provenance record alongside the series name
and the date range. "Consumer confidence was 69" is not a fact until you say
which measure, constructed how. Two correct numbers describing the same
reality can differ by thirty points, and neither is wrong.

```{python}
#| label: cci-provenance
print("Series     : USACSCICP02STSAM")
print("Name       : Consumer Opinion Surveys: Composite Consumer Confidence,")
print("             United States")
print("Source     : OECD, via Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED)")
print("Units      : Percentage balance, seasonally adjusted")
print("Frequency  : Monthly")
print(f"Date range : {cci.date.min().date()} to {cci.date.max().date()}")
print(f"Rows       : {len(cci):,}")
```

### An observation worth investigating

```{python}
#| label: cci-record-low
low = cci.cci.min()
low_date = cci.loc[cci.cci.idxmin(), "date"]
rank = (cci.cci <= low).sum()

print(f"Lowest reading in the series: {low:.2f} in "
      f"{low_date.strftime('%B %Y')}")
print(f"That is the lowest of {len(cci):,} monthly observations "
      f"going back to {cci.date.min().year}.")
print()
print("Ten lowest readings on record:")
print(cci.nsmallest(10, "cci").assign(
    month=lambda d: d.date.dt.strftime("%b %Y"))[["month", "cci"]]
    .to_string(index=False))
```

Consumer confidence is at its lowest recorded level in more than sixty years
of this survey — below 2008, below 2020. Look at where the other low readings
cluster and what was happening then.

::: {.charcoal}
**A question to think about.** Consumer confidence measures how households
*feel* about the economy. Other indicators — employment, asset prices, output
— measure what is *happening* to it. These usually move together. When they
diverge sharply, one of three things is true: the sentiment measure is picking
up something the hard data has not registered yet, the hard data is capturing
something sentiment ignores, or the two are responding to different events
entirely.

Which chart would you build to tell them apart? What would you need on the
same axis, and over what period?
:::

The discontinued series is `CSCICP03USM665S`; the current one is
`USACSCICP02STSAM`. If you had built a forecast on the first one in early 2024
it would have looked fine, right up until someone asked what happened last
quarter.

We use the current series from here on.

```{python}
#| label: stem-leaf
recent = cci[cci.date >= cci.date.max() - pd.DateOffset(years=2)]
print(f"Consumer confidence, {recent.date.min().strftime('%B %Y')} "
      f"to {recent.date.max().strftime('%B %Y')}\n")
_ = stem_and_leaf(recent["cci"])
```

Read down the stems to see where readings cluster. Unlike a histogram, every
individual observation is still there — you can recover the actual values,
which is why Tukey liked it and why it survives in exploratory work.

```{python}
#| label: cci-extremes
print(f"Lowest reading:  {cci.cci.min():.2f} in "
      f"{cci.loc[cci.cci.idxmin(), 'date'].strftime('%B %Y')}")
print(f"Highest reading: {cci.cci.max():.2f} in "
      f"{cci.loc[cci.cci.idxmax(), 'date'].strftime('%B %Y')}")
print(f"Most recent:     {cci.cci.iloc[-1]:.2f} in "
      f"{cci.date.iloc[-1].strftime('%B %Y')}")
```

## Scatter plots

A **scatter plot** displays two variables with no summarising at all. Every
observation is shown. Most analysts draw one first when meeting a new data set.

### Which variable goes on which axis

Before drawing one you have to decide which variable goes where, and the
convention carries a claim.

The **independent variable** goes on the horizontal axis. It is the one you
are treating as given. The **dependent variable** goes on the vertical axis.
It is the one you believe responds:

$$\text{independent } (x) \;\longrightarrow\; \text{dependent } (y)$$

The arrow only points one way. The textbook's example is television size and
price: bigger televisions cost more, so size is $x$ and price is $y$ — and
cutting the price of a television does not shrink it.

::: {.charcoal}
Notice what you have just done. Putting population growth on the horizontal
axis and house price growth on the vertical is a *decision about which one you
think responds to which*, and it is made before any statistics happen. Nothing
in the data forces it. Someone who believes people move toward places where
prices are already rising would draw the axes the other way round and get an
identical-looking cloud with an identical correlation.

The axis convention is where regression begins — Chapter 10 will ask you to
defend the choice rather than assume it. For now: make the choice
deliberately, and say out loud that you made it.
:::

### The same states, two variables, one substitution

```{python}
#| label: scatter-pair
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6))
for ax, (col, label) in zip(axes, [("HPI", "House price INDEX LEVEL"),
                                   ("gHPI", "House price CHANGE over the decade (%)")]):
    ax.scatter(states["gPOP"], states[col], color=UNLV_SCARLET, alpha=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("Population growth over the decade (%)")
    ax.set_ylabel(label)
    ax.set_title(f"{label}\nr = {states[col].corr(states['gPOP']):+.3f}", fontsize=10)
    ax.grid(color="#e6e6e6")
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The left panel is a cloud. The right panel is a relationship. The horizontal
axis is identical in both; only the vertical variable changed, and it changed
from an index level to a percentage change of that same index.

**A scatter plot cannot rescue a badly chosen variable — but it shows you
faster than anything else that you have chosen one.** This is why analysts draw
scatter plots first.

### Time series

A scatter plot where one variable is time shows a *time path*. Connecting the
points produces a **line chart**, which is normally the right way to show a
time series.

```{python}
#| label: cci-timeseries
_ = time_series(cci["date"], cci["cci"],
                title="US consumer confidence index",
                ylab="Index")
```

```{python}
#| label: recession-timeseries
annual = (recessions.set_index("date")["recession"]
          .resample("YS").mean().reset_index())
_ = time_series(annual["date"], 100 * annual["recession"],
                title="Percent of days in recession, by year",
                ylab="Percent of days")
```

## Charts that mislead

Everything below is technically correct and still misleading. These are the
failures to watch for — in other people's charts, and in your own.

### Truncating the axis

```{python}
#| label: truncated-axis
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

subset = states.nlargest(6, "gHPI")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))

for ax, (lo, hi), label in zip(
        axes, [(0, None), (subset.gHPI.min() - 5, None)],
        ["Axis starts at zero", "Axis starts near the minimum"]):
    ax.bar(subset["Member"], subset["gHPI"], color=UNLV_SCARLET, alpha=0.85)
    ax.set_ylim(lo, hi)
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.set_ylabel("House price growth over the decade (%)")
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6")
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Highest: {subset.gHPI.max():.1f}%   "
      f"Lowest of these six: {subset.gHPI.min():.1f}%")
print(f"Actual gap between them: {subset.gHPI.max() - subset.gHPI.min():.1f} "
      f"percentage points")
```

Same six states, same six numbers. The right-hand chart makes the gap look
enormous. For bar charts, where length encodes the value, the axis should start
at zero.

### Letting bin width choose the story

```{python}
#| label: bin-width
for k in [3, 6, 15]:
    print(f"\n--- {k} bins ---")
    t = frequency_table(states["gPOP"], bins=k)
    print(t.to_string(index=False))
```

```{python}
#| label: bin-width-charts
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
for ax, k in zip(axes, [3, 6, 15]):
    ax.hist(states["gPOP"], bins=k, color=UNLV_SCARLET, alpha=0.85,
            edgecolor="white")
    ax.set_title(f"{k} bins")
    ax.set_xlabel("Population growth (%)")
    ax.grid(axis="y", color="#e6e6e6")
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three bins say the distribution is smooth. Fifteen bins say it is lumpy and
possibly bimodal. Same fifty states. **Nobody looking at one histogram can tell
you which bin width you tried first.**

### The wrong chart for the data

```{python}
#| label: wrong-chart
top = states.nlargest(8, "POPN")
_ = pie_chart(top["Member"], top["POPN"],
              title="Population of the eight largest states")
```

Eight slices. Try ranking the third, fourth, and fifth largest by eye, then
check against the bar chart.

```{python}
#| label: right-chart
_ = bar_chart(top["Member"], top["POPN"],
              title="Population of the eight largest states",
              xlab="State", ylab="Population (thousands)")
```

### What to check in any chart

::: {.charcoal}
1. **Does the axis start at zero?** Required for bars; often wrong for lines.
2. **What is the base?** Percent *of what*, and who was excluded.
3. **How many observations per bar or cell?** A tall bar over four
   observations is noise.
4. **Would a different bin width tell a different story?**
5. **How old is the data?** Check the last observation date.
6. **Does the caption claim more than the chart shows?** Correlation drawn as
   a chart is still correlation.
:::

## Building it in Excel, with Claude

Roughly a third of the textbook chapter is Excel choreography. Activate the
Data Analysis ToolPak. Array-enter `=FREQUENCY(A2:A51,C2:C7)` with
Ctrl+Shift+Enter. Delete the "More" row Excel adds. Right-click a bar, open
Format Data Series, drag Gap Width to 0%. Right-click the red bars, Change
Series Chart Type to Line. Set the axis maximum from 1.2 to 1.0.

That is about forty clicks per chart, and every one of them belongs to a
version of Excel's user interface rather than to statistics. You will not be
assessed on any of it.

::: {.scarlet}
**The clicks were never the skill. The specification is the skill, and the
specification is statistics.**

Every decision the textbook labours over — how many classes, where the
boundaries fall, whether they are mutually exclusive, whether all $n$ values
are accounted for, whether the bars touch, whether a pie chart is even the
right chart — is exactly what you have to *tell* an assistant, and exactly
what you have to *check* when it hands the workbook back.
:::

### A loose prompt and what it returns

Start here, because you will be tempted to:

> Make me a frequency distribution of this data in Excel.

**[Download `ch02-frequency-BROKEN.xlsx`](../upload_packs/lab-2-chapter-02/ch02-frequency-BROKEN.xlsx)**
and open it. That is what came back. It has a tidy table, a chart, and six
classes. Everything in it is correct arithmetic.

Open the **Checks** sheet before you look at anything else.

Three things went wrong, and none of them is visible in the chart:

1. **Nothing is a formula.** Click cell `D5`. It is the number `5`, typed in.
   Change a class boundary in column B and watch the table not move.

2. **The class boundaries were never rounded.** They came straight out of
   $(\max - \min) / 6 = 4.5$ and read "−4.20 to 0.30". Donnelly p.34 is
   explicit: round the estimate to a readable whole number. Nobody can hold
   "−4.20 to 0.30" in their head.

3. **The boundaries include both endpoints**, so a state sitting exactly on
   one lands in two classes. South Carolina grew 13.8% — exactly the fourth
   boundary — so it is counted twice. **Fifty states, fifty-one observations.**
   That is the textbook's rule 2, broken.

None of this required the assistant to make anything up. It answered the
question it was asked. The question was underspecified.

### A prompt that names every decision

::: {.prompt}
Prompt

> Build me an Excel workbook from `state_hpi_ur_pop.csv`.
>
> **Sheet 1, `Data`:** the raw file, headers in row 1, nothing else.
>
> **Sheet 2, `Distribution`:** a frequency distribution of the `gPOP` column.
> Use six classes of width 5 running from −5 to 25. Columns: class label,
> lower bound, upper bound, frequency, relative frequency, cumulative relative
> frequency, plus a total row.
>
> Classes must be **mutually exclusive**: half-open, "at least the lower bound
> and strictly less than the upper", so no state can fall in two classes.
>
> Use **live Excel formulas** throughout — `COUNTIFS` referencing the bound
> cells, `SUM` for the total. No pasted values anywhere: I want to change a
> bound and watch the table and the charts update.
>
> **Sheet 3:** a histogram of that distribution with **no gaps between the
> bars** — the data are continuous — with the axis starting at zero and both
> axes labelled; and an ogive of the cumulative relative frequency.
>
> Finally, tell me which cells hold formulas and which hold constants.
:::

Read that back and notice what it is. It is not a description of a
spreadsheet. It is the whole of section 2.2: the number of classes, the class
width, the boundary rule, the gap convention. **You cannot write that prompt
without knowing the statistics.** That is the point, and it is why the prompt
is the assessed artefact rather than the workbook.

**[Download `ch02-frequency-FIXED.xlsx`](../upload_packs/lab-2-chapter-02/ch02-frequency-FIXED.xlsx)**
to see what comes back.

### The ten-second demonstration

Open the fixed workbook and change **one cell**: on the `Distribution` sheet,
change `C10` — the top boundary — from 25 to 22.

Idaho grew 22.8%, so Idaho now falls outside every class. The total drops to
49. The last class empties. Both charts redraw. Checks 1 and 6 turn red.

Then look at checks 2 and 3. **They still pass.** The relative frequencies are
computed against the total of the classes, so they quietly renormalise to the
49 states that survived and sum to exactly 1.000. Every percentage on the
sheet is now internally consistent, and describes 49 states while claiming to
describe 50.

::: {.scarlet}
That is the Valentine's Day pie chart again, in a spreadsheet: correct
arithmetic on a base nobody stated.

It is also why the first check compares against $n$ **from the source file**
rather than against the column's own total. A checklist that only asks whether
a sheet agrees with itself will pass this every single time.
:::

Set `C10` back to 25.

### The checklist

Every workbook in this course carries these six checks, as live formulas
rather than as advice. Run them on anything an assistant builds you — and on
anything you build yourself.

| # | Check | Rule it enforces |
|---|-------|------------------|
| 1 | Frequencies sum to $n$, taken from the source file | Include all data values |
| 2 | Relative frequencies sum to 1.00 | |
| 3 | Cumulative column ends at 1.00 | |
| 4 | Frequency cells hold **formulas**, not typed numbers | Change a bound, watch it move |
| 5 | No value falls in two classes | Mutually exclusive classes |
| 6 | No empty classes | |

Six checks, under a minute, and they are all rules from this chapter rather
than rules about software.

### Your turn

**[Download `ch02-frequency-STARTER.xlsx`](../upload_packs/lab-2-chapter-02/ch02-frequency-STARTER.xlsx)**.
It has the data, the class boundaries, and the six checks already wired up.
The frequency, relative frequency and cumulative columns are empty, and every
check reads `-- not yet --` or `FAIL`.

Build the table until all six read `PASS`. Do it by hand, or write the prompt
and have Claude do it — either is fine, and the checks do not care which.
What they care about is that you can tell the difference between a workbook
that is right and a workbook that merely looks right.

::: {.charcoal}
**What to watch for.** These are the failures this particular task produces,
in rough order of frequency:

- Pasted values where you asked for formulas — by far the most common
- Boundaries inclusive at both ends, so the frequencies sum to $n + 1$
- The overflow class silently dropped, so they sum to less than $n$
- Default bins chosen without reference to $2^k \ge n$
- The "Other" slice quietly removed from a pie chart to make it tidier
- A chart title that claims more than the chart shows

Every one of these produces a workbook that opens cleanly and looks
professional. The checklist is how you find out.
:::

### The rest of the chapter's Excel work

The same pattern covers everything else the textbook demonstrates. Each is one
specified prompt and one run of the checklist:

- `COUNTIF` for a frequency distribution of **qualitative** data
- A **PivotTable** as a contingency table — pivot tables are the one Excel
  skill in this chapter you will use every week
- **Clustered** bar charts to compare within a category, **stacked** to compare
  totals across categories
- A **Pareto** chart: sorted bars plus the cumulative line on a secondary axis
- **Sparklines** — one-cell trend lines for a table of time series
